y-m-15-04.title: Wetin we fit know for sure from numbers for table alone?
y-m-15-04.topic: Read table: wetin data show and wetin you no fit know from multiple-choice answers
y-m-15-04.goal: For survey table where one person fit choose several things, sort wetin you fit say for sure and wetin need more information, then make different records wey match same table.
y-m-15-04.material:
24 students for one Grade 5 class answer survey: “Choose all sports you like.” Dem fit choose soccer and basketball, both or neither. All 24 students hand in survey.

| Sport | Number of students wey choose am |
| Soccer | 14 students |
| Basketball | 11 students |
y-m-15-04.thinking.0: Separate statements wey data settle from those wey no settle

y-m-15-04.s.s1.o.b: Number of students wey no choose soccer na 10.

Then y na x minus 1, so (1,0), (2,1), (5,4), (11,10), and so on fit. y-m-15-01.title: If average na 12 books, must one day get 12 books borrowed?
y-m-15-01.topic: Meaning of average: average and real records
y-m-15-01.goal: Make case where no record equal average, to correct idea “average na one of real records” with counterexample, and say wetin average show and no show.
y-m-15-01.material: At Starlight Library, dem record books borrowed each day for 4 days, Monday to Thursday. Average for 4 days na 12 books. Number of books borrowed per day na natural number from 0 to 30. Seoyun talk, “Average na 12 books, so at least one of 4 days must get exactly 12 books borrowed.”
y-m-15-01.thinking.0: Test claim “must be so” with one counterexample
y-m-15-01.thinking.1: Make different records wey meet condition (total)
y-m-15-01.thinking.2: Separate wetin average tell from wetin e no tell
y-m-15-01.prereq.0: Meaning of average: value when all data made equal (Grade 5 level)
y-m-15-01.s.s1.prompt: Wetin surest way to find whether Seoyun “must be so” correct?
y-m-15-01.s.s1.hint.0: Underline “must” in Seoyun statement and think what kind example fit break am.
y-m-15-01.s.s1.hint.1: First decide di total number of books for 4 days must be if average na 12.
y-m-15-01.s.s1.o.a: Make many records wey average 12 and check if dem include a day with 12 books.
y-m-15-01.s.s1.r.a: Many examples wey fit no prove “must.” One opposite example enough to break “must.”
y-m-15-01.s.s1.o.b: Ask librarian whether any of di 4 days get 12 books borrowed.
y-m-15-01.s.s1.r.b: You only learn about these 4 days. You no test statement “if average 12, there must be one day like that” itself.
y-m-15-01.s.s1.o.c: Try make record with average 12 but no day get 12 books.
y-m-15-01.s.s1.r.c: Dis test di word “must” directly. You only need make example wey keep condition but go against statement.
y-m-15-01.s.s1.o.d: Check once more how to find average.
y-m-15-01.s.s1.r.d: Knowing how to calculate different from testing whether “must be so” correct.
y-m-15-01.s.s1.explain: Statement “must be so” become false with just one record wey keep condition but no match. So surest way na make record with average 12 but no day with 12 books.
y-m-15-01.s.s2.prompt: Make 3 different records with average 12 and no day where exactly 12 books borrowed. (Monday m, Tuesday t, Wednesday w, Thursday h.) Records wey only swap days count as same record.
y-m-15-01.s.s2.hint.0: Think wetin happen when some days above 12 and some below. If one day na 2 below 12, how much another day need go up? 12
y-m-15-01.s.s2.hint.1: First make pair like (11, 13), then fit remaining 2 days to the sum.
y-m-15-01.s.s2.ok.c1: All na natural numbers from 0 to 30.
y-m-15-01.s.s2.fail.c1: Books per day must be natural number from 0 to 30.
y-m-15-01.s.s2.fail.c2: Average for 4 days no be 12. Check sum of 4 numbers.
y-m-15-01.s.s2.fail.c3: One day get 12 books borrowed. Change number of books for dat day.
y-m-15-01.s.s2.explain: For example, (10, 11, 13, 14) sum to 48, so average 12, but no day get 12 books. (8, 9, 15, 16) and (0, 30, 9, 9) work too. Average no need be one of real records.
y-m-15-01.s.s3.prompt: Wetin you go tell Seoyun? Explain using numbers from record you just make.
y-m-15-01.s.s3.hint.0: You fit use one record you made for previous step exactly as e be.
y-m-15-01.s.s3.hint.1: First write one sentence, “how Seoyun statement wrong,” then add number example.
y-m-15-01.s.s3.placeholder: Example: That no always true. For example, ...
y-m-15-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: You check again say 4 numbers in record add up to 48?
y-m-15-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: You write am so point “no day get 12” visible from numbers?
y-m-15-01.s.s3.selfAssess.2: You write few words about wetin average tell (value when everything made equal)?
y-m-15-01.s.s3.model.0: That no always true. For example, 10, 11, 13, and 14 books add to 48, so average na 12, but no single day get 12 books.
y-m-15-01.s.s3.model.1: You wrong. 0, 30, 9, 9 books also average 12, but no day get 12. Average na value when all equal, so e fit differ from real records.
y-m-15-01.s.s3.modelNote.1: I give extreme example and connect am to meaning of average.

y-m-15-02.title: If average change after sixth test
y-m-15-02.topic: Find a new average from an average: known average and new data
y-m-15-02.goal: Find and correct mistake wey happen when combining known average with new data to find new average, and find several new scores wey match target average.
y-m-15-02.material: Hajun take math unit test 5 times, and average score na 70 points. All scores na natural numbers from 0 to 100. On sixth test, he score 90. Hajun talk, “Now make we find average of 6 tests,” then solve like below.
y-m-15-02.thinking.0: Find line wey get mistake in solution
y-m-15-02.thinking.1: Ask “how many data values dis average stand for?”
y-m-15-02.thinking.2: Make several new data values wey keep target average
y-m-15-02.prereq.0: Meaning of average (sum ÷ number) and work backwards from average to sum (Grade 5 level)
y-m-15-02.s.s1.prompt: Choose one wrong line in Hajun solution. (Count lines starting from 1.)
y-m-15-02.s.s1.hint.0: For each line, write how many scores di 70 in that line represent.
y-m-15-02.s.s1.hint.1: Work backwards to find total for all 5 scores, then compare am with 80 points wey solution get.
y-m-15-02.s.s1.line.3: Sixth score higher than 70, so average for 6 tests go pass 70.
y-m-15-02.s.s1.explain: Line 3 wrong. 70 points no be one score; na value wey make 5 test scores balance. Problem na say dem count 70 and 90 only once each. Sum for first 5 tests na 70×5=350 points; add 90, total 440; divide by 6 to get about 73.3. Line 4 statement “average go up” correct.
y-m-15-02.s.s2.prompt: Forget 90 points above for a moment and imagine new 6th and 7th tests. After 7 tests, average come out exactly 75. Find 3 different possible pairs for 6th score s and 7th score u. (Both scores natural numbers 0 to 100, and 6th lower than 7th.)
y-m-15-02.s.s2.hint.0: For average of 7 tests to be 75, wetin total of 7 scores must be?
y-m-15-02.s.s2.hint.1: Subtract sum of 5 tests to find sum of other 2 scores, then set one and fit di other.
y-m-15-02.s.s2.ok.c1: Both scores na natural numbers from 0 to 100.
y-m-15-02.s.s2.fail.c1: Scores must be natural numbers from 0 to 100 points.
y-m-15-02.s.s2.fail.c2: Average no be 75. Think again starting from sum of first 5 tests.
y-m-15-02.s.s2.fail.c3: Sixth score must be lower than seventh.
y-m-15-02.s.s2.explain: Sum of 7 scores na 75×7=525 points; sum of first 5 na 350, so 2 remaining scores sum to 175. Pairs totaling 175 where s<u include (75,100), (80,95), (85,90), (87,88), and s fit be anything from 75 to 87. 100 75 80 85 87 88 90 95
y-m-15-02.s.s3.prompt: Explain briefly to Hajun why (70 + 90) ÷ 2 = 80 no fit be average of 6 tests.
y-m-15-02.s.s3.hint.0: First write how many scores 70 points make equal.
y-m-15-02.s.s3.hint.1: If 70 and 90 each count once the same way, compare how many tests each score end up representing.
y-m-15-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: E show say 70 points no be one score, but value wey balance scores for 5 tests?
y-m-15-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: You say where new average go fall between 70 and 90 according to your explanation (whether e closer to 70)?
y-m-15-02.s.s3.model.0: 70 points na average of 5 tests, so sum of those 5 na 350. Add 90 get 440, and divide by 6. If you just divide 2 values by 2, you count first 5 tests like na only one test.
y-m-15-02.s.s3.model.1: 70 points represent 5 tests, but 90 points represent only one test. 80 points, wey count each once, give too little weight to first 5 tests. So correct average should dey closer to 70 than to 80.
y-m-15-02.s.s3.modelNote.1: I explain am with difference in share (weight) without using sum.

y-m-15-03.title: If you draw one blank and put am aside, wetin happen to next person chance?
y-m-15-03.topic: Chance (when drawn slip return to box and when no return)
y-m-15-03.goal: When number of slips in box change, compare and revise chance size based on new information, and separate putting slip back from not putting am back.
y-m-15-03.material: Box get 10 slips same shape and size. 2 slips “winner” and 8 “blank.” After shaking well, people take turns closing eyes, drawing one slip, then opening am. Everybody fit see result. Box contents change at each step below.
y-m-15-03.thinking.1: Compare size by considering total number and number of winners together
y-m-15-03.thinking.2: Separate results wey depend on condition (whether slip put back)
y-m-15-03.prereq.0: Say chance as size of “one part of the whole”; compare fraction sizes (Grade 5 level)
y-m-15-03.prereq.1: Chance words: impossible, even chance, certain
y-m-15-03.s.s1.prompt: New information dey show one step at a time. Each time, choose wetin you think about di chance.
y-m-15-03.s.s1.hint.0: For each step, first count how many slips dey in box now and how many be winners.
y-m-15-03.s.s1.hint.1: Put picture of box from previous step beside current one and find wetin change.
y-m-15-03.s.s1.st.0.info: Jiu wan draw first. Box get 10 slips and 2 winners.
y-m-15-03.s.s1.st.0.ask: Wetin correct way to describe chance say Jiu go draw winner?
y-m-15-03.s.s1.st.0.after: 2 of 10 slips na winners, so na 1/5 of whole. Correct to say chance lower than even chance (1/2) and not impossible (0). Also “about one in five” only describe size of chance; e no mean one of every 5 draws must be winner.
y-m-15-03.s.s1.st.0.o.a: Only 2 winners dey, so Jiu wey draw first no fit win.
y-m-15-03.s.s1.st.0.r.a: Low chance and impossible no be same. Winning slips dey inside box.
y-m-15-03.s.s1.st.0.o.b: Winners fewer than blanks, so chance below even but no be impossible.
y-m-15-03.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You compare number of winners and blanks to describe chance size. You put am correctly between impossible and certain.
y-m-15-03.s.s1.st.0.o.c: Na 2 out of 10, so chance roughly one in five.
y-m-15-03.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You express chance as one part of whole (2/10). E mean same as saying chance low.
y-m-15-03.s.s1.st.0.o.d: Person wey draw first get biggest advantage, so chance of winning high.
y-m-15-03.s.s1.st.0.r.d: Order alone no decide chance. First consider number of winners and total slips in box.
y-m-15-03.s.s1.st.1.info: Slip Jiu draw na blank. Jiu no put am back. Now Harin go draw.
y-m-15-03.s.s1.st.1.ask: How you go compare chance say Harin draw winner with Jiu chance before drawing?
y-m-15-03.s.s1.st.1.after: At first na 2 out of 10, but one blank don go, so now na 2 out of 9. 2/9 small bigger than 2/10. Chance change because we know Jiu result.
y-m-15-03.s.s1.st.1.o.a: Winners still 2 and total now 9, so chance increase small.
y-m-15-03.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You rethink both number of winners and total. You see say one blank leaving change chance.
y-m-15-03.s.s1.st.1.o.b: Jiu take blank away, so now na winner turn to come out and chance increase.
y-m-15-03.s.s1.st.1.r.b: Reason no be “turn”; na because number of slips in box change. Explain using wetin dey inside box.
y-m-15-03.s.s1.st.1.o.c: We no fit know yet. Mixing slips na luck, so we no fit know chance either.
y-m-15-03.s.s1.st.1.r.c: Even if na luck, you fit describe chance size from numbers in box. Count winners and slips wey remain.
y-m-15-03.s.s1.st.1.o.d: Only one slip don go, so chance stay the same.
y-m-15-03.s.s1.st.1.r.d: Total reduce but number of winners stay same. Write fractions and compare dem.
y-m-15-03.s.s1.st.2.info: Harin also draw blank. This time she put slip back inside box and mix well. Doyun dey about to draw. Jiu blank still dey outside box.
y-m-15-03.s.s1.st.2.ask: How you go compare Doyun chance of drawing winner with chance just before Harin draw?
y-m-15-03.s.s1.st.2.after: Harin put back di blank, so box get same 9 slips (2 winners) as before she draw. Chance stay 2/9. If she no put am back, na 2 out of 8, wey higher.
y-m-15-03.s.s1.st.2.o.a: Another blank come out, so chance increase compared with before Harin draw.
y-m-15-03.s.s1.st.2.r.a: Harin put blank back. Count yourself whether number in box reduce.
y-m-15-03.s.s1.st.2.o.b: Na same as when box get 10 slips at beginning. Harin put blank back, so everything return to beginning.
y-m-15-03.s.s1.st.2.r.b: Harin blank return, but Jiu blank still outside. Count slips in box.
y-m-15-03.s.s1.st.2.o.c: Harin don draw too, so number go down.
y-m-15-03.s.s1.st.2.r.c: If she put am back, box same as before Harin draw. Look wetin dey inside box, no be how many people don draw.
y-m-15-03.s.s1.st.2.o.d: Na same as just before Harin draw. Box still get 9 slips, and 2 winners.
y-m-15-03.s.s1.st.2.r.d: You count slips inside box yourself and compare. You point out say when slip return, box look same as before.
y-m-15-03.s.s1.reflect: How di chance you first think about change or stay same at each step? Which information change am, and which no change am?
y-m-15-03.s.s2.prompt: Use slip numbers explain how next person chance differ if blank no return to box and if e return.
y-m-15-03.s.s2.hint.0: Write number of slips in box when one blank dey outside and when dem put am back.
y-m-15-03.s.s2.hint.1: Check whether number of winning slips same or different in both cases.
y-m-15-03.s.s2.placeholder: Example: If dem no put am back, ...
y-m-15-03.s.s2.selfAssess.0: When dem no put am back, you write which one change, total slips or number of winners?
y-m-15-03.s.s2.selfAssess.1: For case where dem put am back, you write wetin box look like?
y-m-15-03.s.s2.selfAssess.2: E clear whether chance you write become bigger than at start (2/10) or stay same?

y-m-15-03.s.s2.model.1: If you put blank back inside, box return to how e be, so chance stay 2/10. If you no return am, e change to 2/9 and go up small.

y-m-15-05.title: If we ask 20 students to learn wetin 100 students think
y-m-15-05.topic: Collect data: compare ways to choose who to survey
y-m-15-05.goal: Compare ways to choose a sample when asking everyone hard. Make your own plan to divide people so result no lean one way, and state limits too.
y-m-15-05.material: Grade 5 get Class 1 with 28 students, Class 2 with 26, Class 3 with 24, and Class 4 with 22; 100 all together. Student council wan find “activity students want do pass during break.” No enough time to ask all 100 separately, so dem wan ask only 20. You must choose how to select 20 students from methods below.
y-m-15-05.thinking.0: Compare and judge whether survey method bias one side
y-m-15-05.thinking.2: State both good points and limits of method
y-m-15-05.prereq.0: Experience showing data with tables and bar graphs (Grade 4–5 level)
y-m-15-05.prereq.1: Divide by estimating number: about 1 in 5
y-m-15-05.s.s1.prompt: Choose method wey best show wetin 100 Grade 5 students think from answers of 20 students.
y-m-15-05.s.s1.hint.0: For each choice, check “any student no fit get picked?” Find who no fit ever be chosen.
y-m-15-05.s.s1.hint.1: Compare effect of choosing same number from classes with different numbers of students, like Class 1 and Class 4.

y-m-15-05.s.s1.r.a: Students wey come out to playground fit already lean toward one activity. Students wey dey classroom no fit get picked.
y-m-15-05.s.s1.o.b: For each class, draw number to choose, but choose number from each class based on class size.
y-m-15-05.s.s1.r.b: Every student get chance to be picked, and class sizes also count. E combine 2 ways to reduce bias.
y-m-15-05.s.s1.o.c: Choose one class and ask 20 students inside am.
y-m-15-05.s.s1.r.c: One class thinking fit differ from others. Students for other classes no get chance.
y-m-15-05.s.s1.o.d: For each class, ask students with attendance number 1 to 5. 20
y-m-15-05.s.s1.r.d: Who get picked don decide by number, so students with number 6 or above no get chance.

y-m-15-05.s.s1.r.e: Dis idea include everybody thinking. E take more time and work, and some students fit no hand in form.
y-m-15-05.s.s1.explain: To avoid bias, every student need chance of getting picked, and class size should count too. So random selection inside each class, with number from each class set according to class size, fit. Asking all 100 with questionnaire also possible, but short-time condition limit am.

y-m-15-06.title: If box get most red marbles, red most likely to come out?
y-m-15-06.topic: Compare chance: having more items versus having bigger chance
y-m-15-06.goal: When comparing marble boxes, confirm and explain with counterexample say compare red share of whole, no be just number of red marbles.
y-m-15-06.material:
Three boxes get marbles same size and shape. For each box, close eyes and take one marble. Every marble red or blue.

| Box | Total marbles | Red marbles |
| 가 | 5 | 4 |
| 나 | 10 | 7 |
| 다 | 8 | 5 |

Yuna talk, “Box 나 get most red marbles, 7, so red most likely come out from box 나.”
y-m-15-06.thinking.1: Make counterexample where more items but lower chance
y-m-15-06.prereq.0: Write part of whole as fraction; compare fraction sizes (Grade 5 level)
y-m-15-06.prereq.1: Meaning of drawing with eyes closed: every marble get equal chance of being picked
y-m-15-06.s.s1.prompt: Which box get highest chance of drawing red marble?
y-m-15-06.s.s1.hint.0: For each box, write “how many of all marbles are red” as fraction in same form.
y-m-15-06.s.s1.hint.1: Change fractions to decimals or make denominators same, then compare sizes.
y-m-15-06.s.s1.o.a: Box 나 (because e get most red, 7)
y-m-15-06.s.s1.r.a: You look only red count being largest. Total marbles differ between boxes. Compare red share of whole box.
y-m-15-06.s.s1.o.b: Box 가, because red take biggest share of all marbles
y-m-15-06.s.s1.r.b: You judge by share, no count alone. Boxes different sizes still fit compare using same standard.
y-m-15-06.s.s1.o.c: Box 다, because it get fewest blue mixed in, 3
y-m-15-06.s.s1.r.c: You look only blue count. Even little blue can change red share if total small.
y-m-15-06.s.s1.o.d: All 3 boxes same, because all get red
y-m-15-06.s.s1.r.d: Just having red no allow compare chances.
y-m-15-06.s.s1.explain: Red chance compare by red share of all marbles. Box 가 get 4 of 5, 4/5=0.8; Box 나 get 7/10=0.7; Box 다 get 5/8=0.625. So 가 highest.
y-m-15-06.s.s2.prompt: Make 3 different cases where “box with more red also has higher red chance” wrong. First box r1/t1 (r1 red out of t1 marbles), second r2/t2. First get more red but lower chance. Total marbles 20 or less; first box must get at least 1 blue.
y-m-15-06.s.s2.hint.0: Make first box total big and red count only a bit more than second box.
y-m-15-06.s.s2.hint.1: Write red share of both boxes as decimals and check first one smaller.
y-m-15-06.s.s2.ok.c1: Marble counts natural and 20 or less.
y-m-15-06.s.s2.fail.c1: Marble counts must be natural; each box total at most 20. Second box must get at least 1 red.
y-m-15-06.s.s2.ok.c2: Red count no pass total, and first box get blue too.
y-m-15-06.s.s2.fail.c2: Red no fit exceed total; first box must get at least 1 blue.
y-m-15-06.s.s2.fail.c3: First-box red count must be greater than second-box count.
y-m-15-06.s.s2.ok.c4: Chance of red from first box lower.
y-m-15-06.s.s2.fail.c4: r1/t1 for first box must be less than r2/t2 for second. Compare shares.
y-m-15-06.s.s2.explain: For example, first box 7 red of 10 (0.7), second 4 red of 5 (0.8): first get more red but lower chance. 6/15=0.4 vs 4/5=0.8, 5/12 and 2/3, and 9/20 and 5/8 work too.
y-m-15-06.s.s3.prompt: Explain to Yuna what to compare for chances, using example you made or box 가 and 나 values.
y-m-15-06.s.s3.hint.0: First say in words which of 가 or 나 make red easier to get, then support with numbers.
y-m-15-06.s.s3.hint.1: Think too what you can compare if both boxes get same total marbles.
y-m-15-06.s.s3.placeholder: e.g. Don't only look at red count, because ...

y-m-15-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Your explanation get idea “compare with the whole”?
y-m-15-06.s.s3.selfAssess.2: You think when more red mean same as higher chance? When totals same.
y-m-15-06.s.s3.model.0: No look only red count. Box 가 get 4/5, so red more likely than Box 나 with 7/10. Compare red share of all marbles.

y-m-15-06.s.s3.modelNote.1: I mention too when comparing counts alone is okay (same total).

y-m-15-07.title: Why bar lengths look different for same scores?
y-m-15-07.topic: Read bar graphs: where vertical scale start and impression from bar length
y-m-15-07.goal: Know bar lengths for same data look different depending on vertical-scale start; find and correct reading that misleads, and write title that informs without misunderstanding.
y-m-15-07.material:
Grade 5 class test average: Class 1 82 points, Class 2 85. You draw same data in 2 bar graphs for class newspaper. Bars rise from bottom.

Graph ㉮: vertical scale starts 0 and goes to 100 points, 10 points per interval.
Graph ㉯: scale starts 80 and goes to 90, 1 point per interval. Part below 80 not drawn; bars show only above 80.
Doun look at graph ㉯ and explain like this.
y-m-15-07.thinking.1: Judge what action needed if graph printed as-is
y-m-15-07.prereq.0: Read vertical scale and bar height (Grade 4 level)
y-m-15-07.prereq.1: Compare how many times one number is another (multiplication/division relation)
y-m-15-07.s.s1.prompt: Choose wrong line in Doun explanation. (Line count starts at 1.)
y-m-15-07.s.s1.hint.0: Explain in words, without picture, if part of ㉯ bars below 80 visible.
y-m-15-07.s.s1.hint.1: Put Class 2 and Class 1 scores side by side and estimate how many times one is the other.
y-m-15-07.s.s1.line.0: In graph ㉯, scale start 80 and each interval 1 point.
y-m-15-07.s.s1.line.2: 5 intervals 2.5 times 2, so Class 2 score 2.5 times Class 1.
y-m-15-07.s.s1.line.3: In graph ㉮, difference in bar lengths look tiny compared with bar heights.
y-m-15-07.s.s1.explain: Line 3 wrong. Graph ㉯ shows only above 80, so ratio 5 to 2 (2.5 times) no be score ratio. Compare actual 85 and 82: about 1.04 times, almost same. Line 4 correct. In ㉮ starting at 0, bars look almost same length.
y-m-15-07.s.s2.prompt: You wan print ㉯ in paper. Choose all ways to stop friends misreading am.
y-m-15-07.s.s2.hint.0: For each option, think if e make reader more or less likely to judge only by bar length.
y-m-15-07.s.s2.hint.1: Find method wey show real score gap 82 to 85.
y-m-15-07.s.s2.o.a: Write scale starts at 80, or put break mark below scale
y-m-15-07.s.s2.r.a: Say where scale start help reader no confuse bar length with score itself.
y-m-15-07.s.s2.o.b: Color only Class 2 bar dark so e stand out
y-m-15-07.s.s2.r.b: Different color make bar-length impression stronger. No reduce misunderstanding.
y-m-15-07.s.s2.o.c: Switch to graph ㉮, scale starts at 0
y-m-15-07.s.s2.r.c: If scale starts at 0, bar-length ratio closer to score ratio.
y-m-15-07.s.s2.o.d: Title: “Class 2 is 2.5 times higher than Class 1”
y-m-15-07.s.s2.r.d: This wrongly read bar-length ratio as score ratio.
y-m-15-07.s.s2.o.e: Write scores 82 and 85 on the bars too
y-m-15-07.s.s2.r.e: Showing numbers let readers read values directly instead of judging length only.
y-m-15-07.s.s2.explain: Tell scale start (a), change to 0 (c), and put numbers (e) all reduce bar-length misunderstanding. Dark color (b) or “2.5 times” title (d) make it worse.
y-m-15-07.s.s2.acc.0: Printing ㉯ as-is while also saying scale start and scores also reduce misunderstanding. Better yet combine with graph starting at zero. 0
y-m-15-07.s.s2.acc.1: Changing scale to zero and showing scores too is suitable. 0
